12940-the-chums-of-scranton-high-out-for:
Donald Ferguson's Chums of Scranton High Out for the Pennant follows Hugh and his schoolmates through the Three Town League season. Rain spoils practice before a Saturday game with Belleville, and rivals from Belleville and Allandale look stronger than last year. A man with a cough, a barnacle who came to stay, and Hugh's fade-away ball add plot threads.

A wanderer who talks a blue streak, claiming land in Brazil and the American West before wanderlust pulled him on, shows Ferguson's chatty style. The pennant race builds to a glorious finish. The book offers school baseball with mystery and humour for young readers.
15045-autobiography-letters-and-literary:
Edited by A. Hayward and issued in London in 1861, this two-volume set gathers the life writings of Hester Lynch Piozzi, once Hester Thrale, friend of Samuel Johnson. Her autobiography, letters, and diary extracts, known as Thraliana, sit beside Hayward's notes and an opening account of her life. A second edition added much fresh diary material.

Through Streatham days, Johnson's circle, and her later years, Piozzi writes with wit, candor, and a sharp eye for talk. Hayward's notes place names and events for readers who know Johnson less well. The set remains a key source for Johnson's world, seen through the eyes of a woman who lived close to its center.
23959-fair-italy-the-riviera-and-monte-c:
W. Cope Devereux, a Royal Navy officer and fellow of the Royal Geographical Society, published Fair Italy, The Riviera and Monte Carlo in London in 1884. The volume comprises a tour through north and south Italy and Sicily, with a short account of Malta, and is affectionately dedicated to his wife, in remembrance of their happy tour.

Devereux admits the presumption of writing fresh about a land so often and so well described in prose and verse. Fair Italy, he writes, is the land of song and the cradle of the arts. His earlier book told of a cruise in the Gorgon in the suppression of the slave trade. Here he turns from the sea to the road, the Riviera, and the casino town.
35524-contemporary-belgian-poetry-select:
Contemporary Belgian Poetry gathers verses turned into English by Jethro Bithell. Bithell lectured in German at Birkbeck College, London, in those years. The book came out in the year 1911 and opens with a sonnet. That sonnet honours Émile Verhaeren, the master to whom it is given. Let the dead past fall into the deep, the sonnet begins boldly.

Sylvain Bonmariage opens the contents with an autumn evening in the orchard. Thomas Braun lends benedictions of the ring, of wine, and of cheeses. Isi-Collin, Jean Dominique, and Max Elskamp stand among the names gathered. Elskamp's Mary poems repeat their titles like beads on a string. Verhaeren's iron rimes and battle-song set the tone for the set. The new Belgium of anvils and smoke stands against the old songs.
47703-wilford-woodruff-fourth-president-:
Matthias F Cowley prepared Wilford Woodruff for publication at Salt Lake City in nineteen hundred and nine. Woodruff was the fourth president of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The book gives his life and labours as set down in his daily journals.

Woodruff kept a careful record all his long life, of his own days and of church affairs. His journals ran to thousands of pages, and church writers drew on them for facts. Cowley read them all and chose what mattered most. Parts had already run in the Deseret News and in Leaves from My Journal. The life is given to Woodruff's growing family.
48740-the-book-of-old-fashioned-flowers-:
The Book of Old Fashioned Flowers praises plants that thrive in open air England, by Harry Roberts. Lane published it in London and New York in nineteen o one. It forms number four of a series of handbooks of practical gardening. Roskruge drew its pictures, from poppy anemones to Shirley poppies in bloom.

Roberts dedicates the book to homely folk who love homely, plain flowers. Chapters walk the garden through winter, spring, June, July, and autumn in turn. A garden by the sea and cottage gardens get chapters of their own. Roses, shelter and shade, soils, and manures follow in the working part. Seed sowing, layers, cuttings, weeds, and pests close the gardener's course. The opening scolds handbook writers who preach practice while knowing only books.
6579-men-women-and-god-a-discussion-of-s:
Herbert Gray writes, at the request of the Student Christian Movement, for young men and women of student age. He speaks from long, happy work among students, and says plainly that many need timely, wholesome thought on sex, love, and marriage. His wife, his chief teacher for twenty-five years, gets the book's warm dedication.

Gray treats sex as part of a Christian life, not as a shameful secret, and urges candor, care, and respect between men and women. A brother's appendix adds medical counsel to the pastoral talk. Men, Women, and God is a frank, old-style guide for students who seek a faith-based view of love and sex.
autobiography-letters-and-literary-remai:
Hester Lynch Piozzi, long known as Mrs. Thrale of Streatham, speaks in this collection of her autobiography, letters, and literary remains. A. Hayward edited the second edition, published at London in 1861 in two volumes, with notes and an account of her life and writings. Piozzi was Samuel Johnson's close friend and hostess, and her papers are a prime source for his circle.

Hayward warns that a first edition of such a work is almost bound to be imperfect, since publication revives memories and draws new material. The text obliges: wills, attorneys' bills, and marriage settlements over the Thrale estate appear in footnoted detail. Johnsonians mine these volumes for the Streatham years, her second marriage to Gabriel Piozzi, and the sharp voice that also wrote the famous Anecdotes of Johnson.
britannica-1911-ahr:
Ahr, a river of Germany, is described in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a left-bank tributary of the Rhine, a stream flowing into the Rhine from its left side. The Ahr joins the Rhine at Sinzig. It rises in the Eifel mountains and runs for fifty-five miles in all.

The upper course passes through rather monotonous country, the entry admits. From the village of Altenahr onward, the river's character changes completely. Ruins of the tenth-century castle of Ahr, or Are, tower over that village. Below it the valley becomes a stretch of romantic beauty. The river is well stocked with trout. Steep slopes along the lower valley produce red wines of excellent quality, which give the Ahr much of its fame beyond Germany.
britannica-1911-ak-shehr:
Ak Shehr, ancient Philomelion, is a town in Asia Minor, in the Konia district. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it at the edge of a rich plain below Sultan Dagh. It began likely as a Pergamene town on the great east road from Ephesus. A letter on the death of Polycarp was sent to its people from Smyrna.

Cicero dated letters there on his way to Cilicia in his time. The town played a large part in border wars between Byzantium and Rum. It grew into a key Seljuk town and passed to Ottoman hands later. Turks honor it as the burial place of Nur ed din Khoja.
britannica-1911-bahr: Bahr is the Arabic word for sea, its diminutive form being bahira. The word also means a river, above all a river carrying a large body of water, the Nile being the standing example. In a further use, bahr can name the dry bed of a river, the channel left when the water is gone. The short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry records these senses together: open sea, great river, and the empty riverbed that keeps a river's shape.
britannica-1911-bashahr:
Bashahr, also spelled Bisahir, is a Rajput hill state in the Punjab described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lay amid the Himalayan mountains and covered 3820 square miles. Its population in 1901 was 80,582. The state was large in land and thin in people compared with the plains states of India. Its own figures make that mountain pattern plain.

Government trouble closes the short account. In 1898 the raja, the state's ruler, was judged of weak intellect and had no heir, so a British official took over the administration. In 1906 local trouble broke out because the people refused to pay taxes. Revenue came chiefly from land and from forests, and the forests were leased to the British government, making timber a mainstay of the state's income alongside the land tax.
britannica-1911-bulandshahr:
Bulandshahr, a town and district of British India, fills a full place entry in the 1911 Britannica. The town sits high on the bank of the Kali Nadi River. Its old name was Baran, and its new name means high town. Fine halls, a bath ghat, a market, and a park came from keen town heads. The town count for nineteen oh one was near nineteen thousand.

The district spreads in a flat plain between the Ganges and Jumna Rivers. A canal from the Ganges waters its fields and bears boats. Farms fill the land, with indigo works and cotton mills in its towns. Khurja is its chief trade hub. Past notes run from a raid in ten eighteen to Mogul rule and its fall.
britannica-1911-landwehr:
Landwehr, the German term for a land defence force, gets a militia entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word means defence of the country in plain German. Its use for a rising of armed men is very old. Old church law books already name such levies of the land. Prussia gave the force its modern form in 1813.

A royal edict that March called up men from eighteen to forty-five. They were men not in the standing army, raised to guard the land. After the peace the landwehr stayed part of the Prussian army. A new plan in 1859 moved its troops to the second line. Austria and Switzerland ran their own forms of the same force.
britannica-1911-mulheim-an-der-ruhr:
Muelheim-an-der-Ruhr is a town of Germany, in the Prussian Rhine province, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its industry. It stands on the Ruhr, a tributary of the Rhine, about seven miles west of Essen, at a crossing of several railways. Its people numbered 93,598 in 1905.

The entry says iron-working is its chief industry, with many blast furnaces, rolling mills, foundries, and engine works. Leather, wool, cotton, tobacco, paper, and beer are also made. A vast traffic in coal moves by river and rail, with trade in timber besides. The town became a town in 1508, once belonged to the duchy of Berg, and passed to Prussia in 1815.
britannica-1911-neuenahr:
Neuenahr is a spa of Germany described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in the Prussian Rhine province, at the foot of a basalt peak in the fair valley of the Ahr. A rail line runs to it from Remagen on the Rhine. Its people numbered 3,388 in 1905, and the town is well laid out with three churches.

The town trades in the red wines of its district. Its fame rests on five alkaline springs, whose waters run from cool to hot. Those waters are held a sure cure for chronic catarrh of the airways, for gout, for rheumatism, and for diabetes. Close by lies the Apollinaris spring, a name known far past the town. The article ends with two German books on the springs and on the means of cure in use at the baths.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-moh:
An entry on Christian Mohr, a German sculptor born at Andernach in 1823 and dead at Cologne in 1888. He worked mainly at Cologne under cathedral architect Zwirner, settling there in 1845 after early ornamental work at Mainz and Koblenz. His first Cologne task was the tomb statuettes of Archbishop Conrad of Hochstaden, founder of the cathedral. Christ, the Evangelists, and fifty-nine angels figure on the south portal in his work.

On Emperor William the First's commission he carved eight statues for the middle hall, and his Saint Peter for the middle portal won a first-class medal at Paris in 1855. Beyond Cologne he made panoramic figures for Düsseldorf and thirty-four emperors for Aachen's town hall. Self-taught for the most part, he was also a collector of classical and German antiquities and wrote on Cologne's glory days and its gate towers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-mohr:
Joseph Mohr was a German priest who restored old vernacular hymns to Catholic worship. Born at Siegburg in 1834, he did more than anyone in the last century to bring back old vernacular hymns. These sturdy melodies and texts, sung by the people before the Reformation, included some from the twelfth century. Sentimental modern hymns had pushed them aside.

At first Mohr worked alone in research, later aided by Bäumker and Dreves. His hymn and prayer books, including Cäcilia and Cantate, reached huge circulations, with Cantate alone in forty-two editions. Several collections became official diocesan hymnals, and Mohr himself wrote genuine hymn tunes of lasting quality. He died at Munich in 1892.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-friedric:
Karl Friedrich Rumohr was an art historian born at Dresden in 1785 and dead there in 1843. He became a Catholic in 1804. Wealth, an unquenchable thirst for knowledge, and a keen sense of form made him a critic of art and social life. Italy drew him often, and his hospitality made him welcome everywhere, even with the kings of Prussia and Denmark.

His Italienische Forschungen, in three volumes, treated the Umbrian-Tuscan school masterfully and prepared the way for a critical art history of Italy. Italian residence also yielded works on rural central and upper Italy and his Drei Reisen nach Italien. Searching study produced his books on Holbein and the woodcut, and on Copenhagen's royal print collection. His humorous Hunde-Füchsestreit and Schule der Höflichkeit, and his Geist der Kochkunst, spread his fame further.
men-women-and-god-a-discussion-of-sex-qu:
The Reverend A. Herbert Gray wrote this guide to sex and marriage at the Student Christian Movement's request. He addresses students and young people directly, and speaks to men and women alike. His brother, Dr. Charles Gray, adds a medical appendix. Gray says plainly that he writes from a Christian point of view.

Gray argues that men and women must understand and help each other. He refuses to teach morality through fear, and leaves disease out of the book on purpose. Women friends advised him on the chapters aimed at women readers. The result is an unusually frank church guide from its era.
nasa-tm-19650019791-the-effect-of-materi:
Richard H Fish and James L Summers at Ames Research Center studied what happens when a fast particle strikes a thin plate. Their test asks a simple question with a hard answer. At what point does the impact just break through? That point is called the threshold condition for penetration, in their terms.

Thin plates of many metals were shot with small aluminum spheres. Speeds ranged from low up to eight and a half kilometers per second. The threshold idea helps judge impact resistance for spacecraft parts. Manned modules, pressure vessels, and fuel tanks all face the same risk from tiny high-speed debris in orbit.
nasa-tm-19680028472-electrical-stress-an:
Vincent R. Lalli of Lewis Research Center checks electric stress in a power unit for a microthruster in this November 1968 memo. Good power gear for propulsion tests was hard to get, he notes. Data from past space work showed some failures came from parts pushed past their safe stress.

Lalli tested the unit to find its worst over-stressed parts. The unit was then changed to remove those weak points. After the fix, it ran non-stop for more than seven thousand hours. The work shows how stress checks can turn a weak unit into a tough one. Small thrusters need power gear that lasts through long tests in space.
the-chums-of-scranton-high-out-for-the-p:
Donald Ferguson wrote this boys' baseball story about Scranton High in the Three Town League. Chapter I opens on a Thursday spoiled by rain. Practice is off, and only one more work-out stands between the boys and Saturday's game with Belleville.

The boys agree they need all the practice they can get. A visitor from Belleville reports that both his club and Allandale are stronger than last year. Each rival, rumor says, has set its heart on winning the championship. The contents promise a man trap, a painful shock for Scranton fans, Hugh's fade-away ball, and a glorious finish. Ferguson builds the tale on school loyalty, close games, and a mystery thread that runs beside the pennant race, in the manner of his other Scranton books.
